conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what happened that brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I took a bunch of tramadol and Phenergan. I didn’t want to feel anything anymore. I was arguing with my mom, and I just couldn’t handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. I’m sorry you’re going through this. You drove yourself here after, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. I knew I needed help. I didn’t want to die, not really. I just wanted the pain to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You did the right thing coming in. In the ER, you had a brief episode where you weren’t breathing well and got a dose of Narcan. You responded quickly, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember waking up confused. Was I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was brief and we caught it. No lasting effects. We’ve been monitoring you closely. Your labs are stable, and your breathing is normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on tramadol for my endometriosis pain. But I know it’s not helping my mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re stopping tramadol now. It can affect your mental health, especially with your history. We’ll manage your pain another way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bipolar disorder for years. I’ve had ECT before during pregnancy. It helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your records show that. Psychiatry has reviewed your case. They recommend restarting ECT, and we agree.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. Last time I had a reaction to Haldol. I felt stiff and couldn’t move well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. You’re allergic to Haldol and a few others. We’ve flagged that. No one will give you those meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been sober since I got pregnant. I used to abuse opioids when I was a nurse. I don’t want to go back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. But you’ve stayed clean, and that’s strong. We’ll make sure your treatment supports that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your head when you arrived to make sure there was no brain injury. It came back normal—no bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was confused at first. I thought maybe something was wrong up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The confusion was likely from the overdose. It’s clearing now. Your repeat labs this morning are good—kidneys, liver, electrolytes all stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I take Seroquel, levothyroxine, ranitidine…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still on levothyroxine for your thyroid and ranitidine for reflux. Seroquel was adjusted—psychiatry lowered it to 150mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower it? Was it causing problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not causing harm, but with your mood instability, they want to balance effectiveness and side effects. You also now have a PRN dose for anxiety—25mg as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been using the lidocaine patch for pelvic pain. Can I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s safe to continue. We’ll also keep your prenatal vitamins and Depo-Provera shot as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still hurt, but I don’t want to rely on opioids again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with your gynecologist on non-opioid options. For now, the patch and other supports should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Slept okay. Still sad, but not as overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs from this morning look even better—creatinine improved, electrolytes normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe for me to go to the psych unit for ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve medically cleared you. No complications from the overdose. You’re stable for transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do before ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to be NPO—nothing to eat or drink—after midnight the night before your first treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Will I be able to go home after ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That will depend on how you respond. The team will reassess after a few sessions. For now, focus on getting treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to the psychiatric unit for ECT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve made a brave choice. Your discharge meds are set: same as before, but tramadol is stopped, and Seroquel is 150mg nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can use the PRN Seroquel if I’m anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, up to four times a day if needed. Keep using your inhaler for asthma, thyroid and reflux meds, and the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will someone help me with my mom? She depends on me, but it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The social worker will follow up. There may be support services to help ease the burden while you focus on recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I don’t want to hurt myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you won’t have to. You’re getting the right care now. Keep reaching out when you’re struggling—it’s a strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and I hope to hear you’re doing well soon.
